statement: To find the third binomial straight line.
heath_proof: Let two numbers AC, CB be set out such that the sum of them AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, but has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Let any other number D, not square, be set out also, and let it not have to either of the numbers BA. AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number. Let any rational straight line E be set out, and let it be contrived that, as D is to AB, so is the square on E to the square on FG; [X. 6] therefore the square on E is commensurable with the square on FG. [X. 6] And E is rational; therefore FG is also rational. And, since D has not to AB the ratio which a square number has to a square number, neither has the square on E to the square on FG the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore E is incommensurable in length with FG. [X. 9] Next let it be contrived that, as the number BA is to AC, so is the square on FG to the square on GH; [X. 6] therefore the square on FG is commensurable with the square on GH. [X. 6] But FG is rational; therefore GH is also rational. And, since BA has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, neither has the square on FG to the square on HG the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore FG is incommensurable in length with GH. [X. 9] Therefore FG, GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore FH is binomial. [X. 36] I say next that it is also a third binomial straight line. For since, as D is to AB, so is the square on E to the square on FG, and, as BA is to AC, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore, ex aequali, as D is to AC, so is the square on E to the square on GH. [V. 22] But D has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore neither has the square on E to the square on GH the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore E is incommensurable in length with GH. [X. 9] And since, as BA is to AC, so is the square on FG to the square on GH, therefore the square on FG is greater than the square on GH. Let then the squares on GH, K be equal to the square on FG; therefore, convertendo, as AB is to BC, so is the square on FG to the square on K. [V. 19] But AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore the square on FG also has to the square on K the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore FG is commensurable in length with K. [X. 9] Therefore the square on FG is greater than the square on GH by the square on a straight line commensurable with FG. And FG, GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and neither of them is commensurable in length with E. Therefore FH is a third binomial straight line.

**Statement:** To find the third binomial straight line.

**Step 1.** Set out two numbers AC, CB such that their sum AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, but has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 2.** Set out a further number D which is not square and has not to either of the numbers BA, AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number.

**Step 3.** Set out a rational straight line E (D10.1.3), and find a straight line FG such that, as the number D is to the number AB, so is the square on E to the square on FG (10.6, Porism).

**Step 4.** Since D : AB = (sq. on E) : (sq. on FG), the square on E has to the square on FG the ratio which a number has to a number; therefore the square on E is commensurable with the square on FG (10.6). Hence E and FG are commensurable in square (D10.1.2), and, E being rational, FG is rational (D10.1.3).

**Step 5.** Since D has not to AB the ratio which a square number has to a square number, neither has the square on E to the square on FG; therefore E is incommensurable in length with FG (10.9).

**Step 6.** Produce FG beyond G (P2), and cut off from the produced part a straight line GH such that, as the number BA is to the number AC, so is the square on FG to the square on GH (10.6 Porism, 1.3). Thus FG, GH lie in a straight line, and FH is their sum.

**Step 7.** Since BA : AC = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on GH), the square on FG is commensurable with the square on GH (10.6), so that FG, GH are commensurable in square (D10.1.2). But BA has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore FG is incommensurable in length with GH (10.9).

**Step 8.** Since D : AB = (sq. on E) : (sq. on FG) and AB : AC = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on GH), ex aequali D : AC = (sq. on E) : (sq. on GH) (5.22). Therefore the square on E is commensurable with the square on GH (10.6), so that E, GH are commensurable in square (D10.1.2) and GH is rational (D10.1.3); and, since D has not to AC the ratio which a square number has to a square number, E is incommensurable in length with GH (10.9).

**Step 9.** Accordingly FG, GH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (Steps 4, 7, 8); therefore the whole FH is a binomial straight line, divided into its terms FG, GH at the point G (10.36).

**Step 10.** Since AB is the sum of AC and CB, AB is greater than AC (CN5); and since BA : AC = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on GH), the square on FG is greater than the square on GH (5.14). Consequently FG is greater than GH (for otherwise the square on FG would not exceed the square on GH), and FG is the greater term of the binomial.

**Step 11.** Bisect FG at M (1.10), and with centre M and distance MF describe the semicircle FLG on FG (P3). Since GH is less than the diameter FG, fit into the semicircle a straight line FL equal to GH (4.1), and join LG (P1). The angle FLG, being in a semicircle, is right (3.31); therefore the square on FG is equal to the squares on FL, LG together (1.47). Denote LG by K; then the square on FG is equal to the squares on GH, K together, that is, the square on FG exceeds the square on GH by the square on K.

**Step 12.** Now AB : AC = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on GH), where AB is composed of AC, CB and the square on FG is composed of the squares on GH, K. Therefore, convertendo, AB : CB = (sq. on FG) : (sq. on K) (5.19, Porism).

**Step 13.** But AB has to BC the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore the square on FG has to the square on K the ratio which a square number has to a square number, and FG is commensurable in length with K (10.9). Thus the square on the greater term FG is greater than the square on the lesser term GH by the square on a straight line K commensurable in length with the greater term FG.

**Step 14.** Moreover, neither of the terms FG, GH is commensurable in length with the rational straight line E set out (Steps 5, 8). Therefore FH is a third binomial straight line (D10.2.3); and it has been found. Q.E.F.
